summary: An archipelagic country in the Atlantic made up of more than seven hundred islands, which became independent from Britain in 1973 and relies mainly on tourism and financial services.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: Protestantism is the main religion of the Bahamas, with Baptists the most numerous, followed by Anglicans and Methodists. In 1648 English Puritans, the 'Eleutheran Adventurers', settled on Eleuthera in search of religious freedom; after the American Revolution, in the 1780s large numbers of Loyalist settlers from the South moved in with their slaves, and freed Black Baptist preachers established churches in the Bahamas, so that the Baptist church took root among residents of African descent.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism was formally established in the Bahamas only in the late 19th century by American Benedictine missionaries, who from the 1890s opened churches and schools in Nassau and the Out Islands. Because the Anglican Church was the official church in the British colonial period, Catholics were long a minority, but Catholic schools have some influence in education.

ranking.name: Other Christians
ranking.description: Other Christian denominations include Pentecostals, Seventh-day Adventists and the Church of God, mostly introduced from the United States in the 20th century and attracting believers through fervent worship and community activities. The Bahamas is geographically close to Florida, and American religious broadcasting and church networks have had a great influence on the expansion of these denominations.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population is very small in the Bahamas, only about 2 percent. Bahamian society has a strong religious atmosphere, the preamble of the constitution mentions 'Christian values', and churches play an important role in the community, in education and in politics, so very few people identify as having no religion.

religion.background: The indigenous Lucayan people of the Bahamas were taken by the Spanish to Hispaniola as forced laborers after Columbus landed in 1492 and were nearly extinct within a few decades. In 1648 English Puritans settled on Eleuthera and Protestantism began to be introduced; in 1718 the Bahamas became a British Crown colony and the Anglican Church became the official church. In the 1780s American Loyalist immigrants and their slaves moved in in large numbers, and the Baptist and Methodist churches developed rapidly among residents of African descent. After independence in 1973 the Bahamas remains a predominantly Christian country, and the churches deeply influence society and political culture.

ranking.name: English (including Bahamian Creole English)
ranking.description: English arrived with English colonization in the 17th century and is the official language of government, education and the media. Most residents use Bahamian Creole English in daily life; it formed in the plantation era from a mixture of the languages of West African slaves and English, and was influenced by the language brought by the Southern Loyalist immigrants from the United States in the 1780s, being close to Gullah of South Carolina in the United States.

ranking.name: Haitian Creole
ranking.description: Haitian Creole speakers are mainly immigrants from Haiti and their descendants. Haiti is not far from the southern end of the Bahamas, and from the second half of the 20th century, because of Haiti's political turmoil and poverty, large numbers of Haitians traveled to the Bahamas by boat in search of work, and some used the Bahamas as a stepping stone to the United States. They make up about one tenth of the population, but have long faced disputes over citizenship and immigration policy.

language.history: The indigenous Lucayans of the Bahamas used a language of the Arawakan family, but it disappeared in the early 16th century with the extinction of the people, leaving only a few words, such as 'hammock' and 'hurricane', which come from the Taíno language group. From 1648 the English colonized the islands and English became the main language. In the 1780s American Loyalists and their slaves moved in, so that Bahamian Creole English was influenced by the Black English of the American South. After independence in 1973 English is the official language, and in the late 20th century Haitian immigrants brought Haitian Creole.

ranking.name: Cracked Conch (Conch Fritters)
ranking.description: Chopped conch meat is mixed into a batter with onion, sweet pepper and celery and fried into golden small balls, often dipped in spicy mayonnaise or lemon sauce.
ranking.history: The conch (queen conch) is the most representative seafood of the Bahamas, already eaten by the indigenous Lucayans, and Bahamians are even nicknamed 'Conchy Joes'. Conch fritters are the signature of street and seaside snack stalls, with many vendors around the Arawak Cay fish market in Nassau. In recent years, because of overfishing, the number of conchs has declined, and the Bahamian government has begun to impose fishing restrictions to protect the resource.

ranking.name: Peas 'n' Rice
ranking.description: Rice is cooked together with pigeon peas, tomato, onion, thyme and salt pork; the rice is a light brown color, and it is the most common side dish.
ranking.history: Peas and rice derives from the tradition of rice and bean dishes that West African slaves brought to the Caribbean, and the pigeon pea itself is native to Africa or India and came to the Americas through the slave trade. In the Bahamas it is almost an essential side dish at every meal, often served with fried fish, roast chicken or stewed meat. It is especially indispensable at Sunday family lunches and is a symbol of Bahamian home cooking.

ranking.name: Guava Duff
ranking.description: Guava pulp is rolled into dough and steamed or boiled, and after slicing it is topped with a sweet sauce made of butter, sugar and rum; it is moist and soft with a rich fruity aroma.
ranking.history: 'Duff' comes from the English tradition of steamed puddings, and English colonists brought the method of boiling puddings wrapped in cloth to the Bahamas. Bahamians replaced the dried fruit of England with the locally abundant guava, creating this dessert that blends the features of both places. It is regarded as the national dessert of the Bahamas and is traditionally enjoyed at festivals and after Sunday lunch, and places such as Eleuthera even hold festivals themed on it.

ranking.name: Johnny Cake
ranking.description: A dense baked bread made from flour, butter, milk, sugar and baking powder; the texture is firm and slightly sweet, and it is often cut into pieces and eaten with stewed fish, soup or souse.
ranking.history: Johnnycake is found in both North America and the Caribbean, and its name may come from 'journey cake', because it keeps well and is suited to carrying with you. In the Bahamas, early fishermen and seamen took johnnycake with them as rations when going to sea. Today it is a common staple of traditional breakfasts and lunches, and is especially suited to eating with stewed fish or souse.

ranking.name: Souse
ranking.description: A clear soup stewed from chicken, pig's trotters or mutton with onion, potato, lime juice, chili and allspice; it is sour, spicy and refreshing.
ranking.history: Souse is found in all the former British colonies of the Caribbean, and 'souse' originally referred to meat pickled in brine or vinegar. In the plantation era slaves were often allotted unpopular parts such as pig's trotters and pig's head, and seasoned them with lime juice and chili to make soup. In the Bahamas it is a traditional Saturday morning breakfast, said to cure a hangover, and is often eaten with johnnycake.
